The meanings of *al-nazi'at*, *al-nashitat*, *al-sabiqat*, *al-sabihat* and *al-mudabbirat* have been disputed. It has been said that they are the angels, and it has been said that they are the stars.

On the view that they are the angels, they are called *nazi'at* (those who pull out) because they pull out the souls of the children of Adam from their bodies. They are called *nashitat* (those who draw out) because they draw the souls out, that is, they bring them out. This is from your saying, "I drew out the bucket from the well" (*nashatt al-dalw min al-bi'r*), when you have brought it out. They are called *sabihat* (those who glide) because they glide in their course, that is, they hasten, so they outstrip one another and then arrange the affairs of the servants, the winds, the rain and other things, as God commands them.

On the view that they are the stars, they are called *nazi'at* because they pull from the east to the west. They are called *nashitat* because they move from one zodiac sign to another. They are called *sabihat* because they glide in the orbit (*falak*), and from this is the verse: ﴿And each in an orbit swims along﴾ [Ya-Sin: 40]. So they outstrip in their motion, and thus they arrange a matter from the science of calculation.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "I know of no disagreement that *al-mudabbirat* (those who arrange) are the angels." Al-Zamakhshari mentioned about them what we have mentioned.

It has also been said regarding *al-nazi'at* and *al-nashitat* that they are the souls, which are pulled out by the meaning of pulling at death, and so they are drawn out of the bodies. It has been said regarding *al-sabihat* and *al-sabiqat* that they are horses and that they are ships.

﴿Gharqan﴾: if we say that *al-nazi'at* are the angels, then there are two views on the meaning of *gharqan*. The first: it is from drowning (*gharq*), meaning that they drown the disbelievers in Hell. The second: it is from excess in a matter (*al-ighraq fi al-amr*), in the sense of going to the utmost in it, meaning that they go to the utmost in pulling out, so they cut through the whole orbit. If we say they are the souls, then it is also from excess, meaning that they go to excess in leaving the body.

Grammatically (*al-i'rab*), *gharqan* is a verbal noun (*masdar*) in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*). *Nashtan*, *sabhan* and *sabqan* are verbal nouns, and *amran* is the direct object. The answer to the oath is omitted, and it is the resurrection of the dead, as indicated by what follows it, which mentions the Hour. It has also been said that the answer is ﴿The day the quaking one quakes, followed by the following one﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 6–7], on the assumption that the emphatic lam has been omitted. It has also been said that the answer is ﴿Indeed in that is a lesson for whoever fears﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 26], but this is far-fetched, because it is distant from the oath, and because it points to the story of Pharaoh rather than to the meaning of the oath.

On the Day the quaker quakes, ﴿the Day the quaking one quakes﴾, followed by ﴿the following one﴾. It has been said: "The quaking one is the first blast of the Trumpet (al-Sur), and the following one is the second blast, because it follows the first; that is why it is called 'the following' (al-radifa), from your saying: 'I followed (radiftu) the thing' when you went after it." In a hadith it is stated that between the two there are forty years. It has also been said: "The quaking one is death, and the following one is the Resurrection." It has also been said: "The quaking one is the earth, from His saying: ﴿the earth and the mountains quake﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 14], and the following one is the sky, because it will split asunder on that Day."

The element that governs "on the Day" (yawma) is omitted, and it is the implied response (al-jawab al-muqaddar, the understood answer of the oath or conditional clause). Its sense is: "You will certainly be resurrected on the Day the quaking quakes." If we take "on the Day the quaker quakes" to be the response itself, then the governing element of "on the Day" is the meaning of His words: ﴿Hearts that Day will be trembling﴾. His words ﴿followed by the following one﴾ are in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). It is also possible that the element governing it is "followed" (tatba'uha): ﴿Hearts that Day will be trembling﴾, meaning: intensely agitated. The words "wajif" and "wajib" have the same meaning. "Hearts" is the subject (mubtada') and "trembling" (wajifa) is its predicate. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Trembling (wajifa) is a qualifier, and the predicate is: ﴿their eyes humbled﴾." ﴿Their eyes humbled﴾ is a metonymy for abasement and fear. The attribution of the eyes to the hearts is a figurative usage (tajawwuz, majaz), and the intended meaning is: "the hearts of their owners."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 79, verse 10–12:

﴿They say: "Shall we indeed be returned to our former state (al-hafirah)? * Even when we are decayed bones?"﴾ This is a report of the words of the disbelievers in this world, and its general meaning is the denial of resurrection. Thus the hamza in His words "a-innā lamardūdūn" (ﷺ... ) is an interrogative of denial. For this reason the scholars agreed on reciting it with two hamzas, except that some of them softened the second and some of them lightened it. They differed regarding "idhā kunnā ʿiẓāman nakhirah." Some of them recited it with one hamza, since it is not a place of interrogation or denial, and some recited it with two hamzas, for emphasis on the preceding denial. Then they differed regarding the meaning of al-hafirah, into three opinions. The first is that it is the first state; it is said: "Fulān returned in his hafirah," meaning he returned to his original condition. So the meaning is: "Indeed we are returned to life after death." The second is that al-hafirah is the earth, in the sense of "maḥfūrah" (that which is dug), so the meaning is: "Indeed we are returned to the surface of the earth after being buried in graves." The third is that al-hafirah is the Fire, and "al-ʿiẓām al-nakhirah" are the decayed, rotten bones. It is also recited as "nākhirah" with an alif and without the alif, and both have the same meaning; however, omitting the alif is more emphatic, because fa'il (nakhir) is more intensive than fa'il (nākhir). It is also said that its meaning is hollow bones through which the wind passes, so that a whistling (nakhīr) is heard from them. The governing element of "idhā kunnā" is omitted, its estimate being "idhā kunnā ʿiẓāman nubʿathu" (when we are bones, will we be raised?). It is possible that the governing element is "mardūdūn fi al-ḥāfirah," but this is permissible only on the recitation of "idhā kunnā" with one hamza as a statement, and not on its recitation with two hamzas, because the interrogative hamza does not govern what comes after it. ﴿They said: "That, then, would be a losing return."﴾ Al-karrah is the return, and al-khāsirah is attributed to loss, like His words "ʿīshatin rāḍiyah" (a pleasing life), meaning possessing pleasure; or the meaning is "its companions are losers." The sense of this statement is that they said: if resurrection is true, then our return is a loss, because we will enter the Fire.

For this reason the scholars agreed on reciting it with two hamzas, except that some of them softened the second and some of them lightened it. They differed regarding "idhā kunnā ʿiẓāman nakhirah." Some of them recited it with one hamza, since it is not a place of interrogation or denial, and some recited it with two hamzas, for emphasis on the preceding denial. Then they differed regarding the meaning of al-hafirah, into three opinions. The first is that it is the first state; it is said: "Fulān returned in his hafirah," meaning he returned to his original condition. So the meaning is: "Indeed we are returned to life after death." The second is that al-hafirah is the earth, in the sense of "maḥfūrah" (that which is dug), so the meaning is: "Indeed we are returned to the surface of the earth after being buried in graves." The third is that al-hafirah is the Fire, and "al-ʿiẓām al-nakhirah" are the decayed, rotten bones. It is also recited as "nākhirah" with an alif and without the alif, and both have the same meaning; however, omitting the alif is more emphatic, because fa'il (nakhir) is more intensive than fa'il (nākhir). It is also said that its meaning is hollow bones through which the wind passes, so that a whistling (nakhīr) is heard from them. The governing element of "idhā kunnā" is omitted, its estimate being "idhā kunnā ʿiẓāman nubʿathu" (when we are bones, will we be raised?). It is possible that the governing element is "mardūdūn fi al-ḥāfirah," but this is permissible only on the recitation of "idhā kunnā" with one hamza as a statement, and not on its recitation with two hamzas, because the interrogative hamza does not govern what comes after it. ﴿They said: "That, then, would be a losing return."﴾ Al-karrah is the return, and al-khāsirah is attributed to loss, like His words "ʿīshatin rāḍiyah" (a pleasing life), meaning possessing pleasure; or the meaning is "its companions are losers." The sense of this statement is that they said: if resurrection is true, then our return is a loss, because we will enter the Fire.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 79, verse 13–14:

﴿Then it will be but a single shout﴾, meaning the blast on the Trumpet (al-Sur) for rising from the graves. This is a statement from God Most High in refutation of those who denied resurrection, as if He is saying: Do not think it is difficult for God, when it is easy for Him. He will only blast once on the Trumpet, and the people will rise from their graves. ﴿And at once they will be upon the awakened earth﴾. Idha (إذا, "then suddenly") here is sudden (fa'iyya), and al-sahira (الساهرة) is the surface of the earth, and the ba' (الباء) is for location (zarfiyya). The meaning is: when the Trumpet is blown, they will be on the earth in the swiftest of ways.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary on Surah al-Nazi'at (79), verse 20:

﴿The greatest sign﴾: the turning of the staff into a serpent, and the bringing forth of the hand white (radiant). He made them one sign because the second follows the first. It is also possible that he intends the first alone.

Then he turned away, striving (﴿ثُمَّ أَدْبَرَ يَسْعَىٰ﴾). The turning away (al-idbar) is a metaphor for turning away from faith, and striving (yas'a) is an expression of his effort in disbelief and in nullifying the command of Musa, peace be upon him. It was also said that it is literal: that is, he rose from his assembly, fleeing from sitting with Musa, or running away from the staff when it became a serpent.

﴿فَحَشَرَ﴾ means he gathered his troops and the people of his kingdom.

﴿فَنَادَىٰ﴾ means he called out to his people and said what he said. It is possible that he called them himself, or that he ordered someone to call them, and the first is more apparent. It is related that he stood among them as a preacher and said what he said.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 79, verse 25:

﴿So Allah seized him with the punishment of the Hereafter and of the first [life].﴾ Al-nakal is a verbal noun (masdar) meaning punishment that deters (tankil), and its governing element (al-'amil) is "akhadhahu Allah" (Allah seized him), since it carries the same sense. It was also said that the governing element is omitted. Al-akhirah is the abode of the Hereafter, and al-ula is this world; so the meaning is the punishment of the Hereafter by the Fire and the punishment of the first [life] by drowning. It was also said: al-akhirah refers to his words, "I am your Lord, the Most High," and al-ula refers to his words, ﴿I know of no god for you other than myself﴾ [al-Qasas: 38]. And it was said the reverse: the meaning is that Allah seized him and punished him for the word of the Hereafter and the word of the first [life].

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 79, verses 27–33:

﴿Are you more difficult to create, or is the sky?﴾ This is a rhetorical question (tawqif) intended as evidence for the Resurrection, for He who created the sky is able to create bodies after they have perished. ﴿He raised its vault high﴾ Al-samk (the height): the thickness of the sky, which is the distance between its lower surface, the one adjoining us, and its upper surface, which adjoins what is above it. Raising it means that He made its extent a journey of five hundred years. It is also said that al-samk is the ceiling. ﴿And He leveled it﴾ That is, He perfected its creation. It is also said: He made it even, with nothing elevated or depressed in it. ﴿And He darkened its night﴾ That is, He made it dark. It is said: "ghatasha al-layl" when the night became dark, and Allah "aghtashahu" (darkened it). ﴿And brought forth its forenoon﴾ That is, He made the light of the sun appear at the time of forenoon (duha). He attributed the forenoon and the night to the sky because they are apparent from it and within it. ﴿And the earth, after that, He spread out﴾ That is, He spread it out (daha). Those who say that the earth is flat and not spherical have used this as evidence. We have mentioned in Surah Fussilat [41:11] the reconciliation between this and His words ﴿Then He turned to the sky﴾. ﴿He brought forth from it its water and its pasture﴾ He attributed the water and the pasture to the earth because they come out of it. If it is asked: why did He say "akhraja" without a conjunction (waw)? The answer: this clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) and an explanation of what precedes it, as stated by al-Zamakhshari. ﴿And the mountains He set firmly﴾ That is, He fixed them. The word "al-jibal" is governed by an implied verb indicated by the apparent one, and likewise "al-ard". ﴿As a provision for you﴾ Its meaning: He did all of that as an enjoyment for you from it. ﴿And for your cattle﴾ Because the children of Adam and the cattle benefit from what has been mentioned.

﴿The Overwhelming [Calamity]﴾ is the Resurrection. It was also said: it is the second blast of the Trumpet. Its derivation is from your saying, "ṭamma al-amr" (the matter rose high and prevailed), when the matter rose above everything and overpowered it.
And hell is brought forth for whoever sees. ﴿And Hell will be brought out for whoever sees﴾, meaning it is displayed to everyone who looks, so that it is hidden from no one.

"Maqam Rabbihi" (the station of his Lord): mentioned in Surat al-Rahman [55:46]. "Wa nahan-nafsa 'an al-hawa" (and restrained the soul from desire): i.e., he held it back from its lusts and its corrupt aims. Some of the wise said: "If you want what is right, look at your desire and oppose it." Sahl al-Tustari said: "None is safe from desire except the prophets and some of the truthful (al-siddiqun)."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 79, verses 42–46:

﴿They ask you about the Hour: when will it arrive?﴾ This was mentioned in al-A'raf [7:187]. ﴿What have you to do with mentioning it?﴾ That is, mentioning its time. The meaning is: you are not concerned in any way with mentioning it. ʿĀʾisha (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would often ask about the Hour, and when this verse was revealed, he stopped." ﴿Its finality rests with your Lord﴾ That is, the ultimate knowledge of it belongs to Him; none knows when it will occur except Him alone. ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾ That is: you were only sent to warn of it, and it is not incumbent upon you to inform of its time. The warning was specified for those who fear it, because they are the ones who benefit from the warning. ﴿On the day they see it, it will seem to them as though they had not remained [in the world or in the graves] except for an evening or its morning.﴾ He informs that when they see the Hour, they will think they had not remained in the world, or in the graves, except for an evening of a day or its morning. He also attached the morning (ḍuḥā) to the evening (ʿashiyya) in the same way because of the close connection between them, since both are within one day.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 79, verses 42–46:

﴿They ask you about the Hour: when will it arrive?﴾ This was mentioned in al-A'raf [7:187]. ﴿What have you to do with mentioning it?﴾ That is, mentioning its time. The meaning is: you are not concerned in any way with mentioning it. ʿĀʾisha (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would often ask about the Hour, and when this verse was revealed, he stopped." ﴿Its finality rests with your Lord﴾ That is, the ultimate knowledge of it belongs to Him; none knows when it will occur except Him alone. ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾ That is: you were only sent to warn of it, and it is not incumbent upon you to inform of its time. The warning was specified for those who fear it, because they are the ones who benefit from the warning. ﴿On the day they see it, it will seem to them as though they had not remained [in the world or in the graves] except for an evening or its morning.﴾ He informs that when they see the Hour, they will think they had not remained in the world, or in the graves, except for an evening of a day or its morning. He also attached the morning (ḍuḥā) to the evening (ʿashiyya) in the same way because of the close connection between them, since both are within one day.
